edition.deck: A BBC investigation documents attacks on Sudan’s hospitals, while fresh reporting tracks the Ukraine Starlink dispute and major developments in UK and Danish public affairs.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential overnight developments and useful fresh reporting. Returning stories are included only where the gather adds a significant update or continuing relevance; disputes and unresolved claims are attributed.

content.headline: BBC investigation finds Sudan’s RSF repeatedly attacked el-Fasher hospitals
content.shortHeadline: BBC investigation finds attacks on Sudan hospitals
content.standfirst: The BBC documents at least 43 attacks on healthcare sites during the siege and takeover of el-Fasher. The UN human rights chief says the findings may amount to war crimes; the RSF rejects the allegations.

image.caption: Medics at el-Fasher’s Saudi Hospital perform a Caesarean by phone light on the day the hospital was bombed.

sources.originalTitle: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds

segments.body: A BBC investigation has documented at least 43 attacks on hospitals and other healthcare sites in el-Fasher between May 2024 and October 2025. It also reports that 55 medical workers were killed, 120 injured and 10 forcibly disappeared or abducted between April 2023 and October 2025.

segments.title: Disputed accounts
segments.body: UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings deeply disturbing, saying attacks on civilian infrastructure may amount to war crimes. The RSF rejects the BBC’s findings, describing the allegations as propaganda. The BBC says it found no independent evidence for claims by an RSF-backed health minister that the South Hospital was being used as a military base.

segments.title: A health system under attack
segments.body: Doctors told the BBC that hospitals and temporary treatment sites were repeatedly struck, forcing staff to move patients and surgery as facilities closed. The RSF has also denied that a massacre took place at Saudi Hospital in October 2025; the WHO condemned reported killings there. Healthcare in el-Fasher is now run by the RSF-backed government, which says some hospitals have reopened.

content.headline: Ukraine’s Starlink access remains disputed despite Trump’s claim it is restored
content.shortHeadline: Starlink access for Ukraine remains in dispute
content.standfirst: Trump says Ukraine’s service is back, but a European official says it is not fully functioning and Zelenskyy had reported limits remained. Responsibility for restricting access to the military-grade system is still unclear.

image.caption: Donald Trump, Elon Musk and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, amid the dispute over Ukraine’s Starshield access.

sources.originalTitle: Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming who in the Ukraine-Starlink row?
Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network

segments.body: Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the military-grade service provided through SpaceX’s Starlink system, has been restricted, affecting Ukrainian drones and air defences, according to Ukrainian officials. Donald Trump said Thursday that the service was running again at full speed, but a senior European official told the Associated Press that it was not fully functioning.

segments.title: Responsibility remains unresolved
segments.body: Trump said Elon Musk had restored the service but would not say whether he had asked him to do so. Musk has said the US government controls Starshield access; US officials have denied ordering restrictions. Reporting on whether Musk or the administration made the decision is conflicting, and the latest accounts do not establish who was responsible.

content.headline: Earthquake in Tibet kills 16 and damages hundreds of homes
content.shortHeadline: Tibet earthquake kills 16 and damages hundreds of homes
content.standfirst: At least 32 people were injured after a magnitude 7.0 earthquake, according to local authorities cited by Reuters. Rescuers have been sent to the epicentre as officials assess the damage.

sources.originalTitle: 16 døde efter kraftigt jordskælv i Tibet

segments.body: A magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck Tibet on Thursday evening local time, killing 16 people and injuring at least 32, according to local authorities reported by Chinese state media and cited by Reuters. At least 339 homes were reported to have collapsed, and the extent of the damage is still being assessed.

A rescue team has been sent to the epicentre, which the US Geological Survey placed 183 kilometres north-east of Nagqu. Train services through the affected area have been suspended, and China’s earthquake authority has activated its second-highest emergency response level.

content.headline: Serbia’s student movement rallies before Sunday’s election
content.shortHeadline: Serbia’s students rally ahead of Sunday’s election
content.standfirst: Hundreds of thousands gathered in Belgrade as a student-led movement prepares to challenge Aleksandar Vučić’s party at the polls. Election monitors have raised concerns about threats, violence and unequal conditions.

image.caption: Crowds gather in Belgrade to support Serbia’s student movement before Sunday’s election.

sources.originalTitle: Hundredtusindvis på gaden i Serbien før afgørende valg

segments.body: Hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Belgrade on Thursday to back Serbia’s student movement, which is standing in Sunday’s parliamentary election against the party of long-time leader Aleksandar Vučić. The movement grew out of protests after 16 people died when a railway-station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024.

segments.title: An uncertain contest
segments.body: The student-backed list says it wants to fight corruption, strengthen independent courts and reduce political influence over the media. Polls have pointed in different directions, while one survey cited by DR gave the movement a narrow lead. Independent monitor CRTA has warned of threats, violence and unequal conditions during the campaign; Serbia’s election commission says the vote is free.

content.headline: Judge orders Trump to give evidence under oath in BBC lawsuit
content.shortHeadline: Trump ordered to give evidence under oath in BBC case
content.standfirst: A Florida judge ordered Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by 11 December or risk sanctions, including possible dismissal of his lawsuit. The case concerns a BBC Panorama edit of his 2021 speech.

image.caption: Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

sources.originalTitle: US judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in $10bn lawsuit against BBC
Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit

segments.body: A US judge has ordered Donald Trump to answer questions under oath by 11 December in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC. The magistrate warned that failure to comply could lead to sanctions, including dismissal of the case. Trump’s lawyers have said he could instead appear in January, but the judge has not accepted that as a substitute for the order.

segments.title: The dispute over the edit
segments.body: Trump’s suit concerns a Panorama episode that joined two parts of his 6 January 2021 speech. The BBC has acknowledged that the edit was misleading and argues the case should be dismissed. The judge also allowed a BBC subpoena to Mar-a-Lago to proceed for discovery; the lawsuit’s claims and the broadcaster’s legal arguments have not been decided.

content.headline: France extends curfews and restricts protests ahead of Saturday rallies
content.shortHeadline: France tightens protest restrictions ahead of Saturday
content.standfirst: Paris is extending a partial curfew and Marseille and Lyon are banning demonstrations as authorities prepare for more protests after last weekend’s riots. The government says it will increase police deployments.

image.caption: Demonstrations in France were followed by disorder and damage last weekend.

sources.originalTitle: Paris extends curfew as Marseille and Lyon ban protests after riots

segments.body: Paris will keep overnight movement restrictions in parts of the city until Monday, while Marseille and Lyon have announced bans on protests this weekend. In other areas, President Emmanuel Macron said only authorised union demonstrations would be allowed where possible. The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in Paris will close on Saturday.

segments.title: Response to last weekend’s unrest
segments.body: The measures follow demonstrations against living costs and school conditions that were marred by looting and damage. France’s justice minister said 217 people had been jailed after fast-track trials and 2,700 arrested. Macron said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared with last weekend; the restrictions and policing plan are intended to prevent further disorder.

content.headline: Yemen’s war and rising prices deepen hunger crisis for children
content.shortHeadline: War and soaring prices worsen Yemen’s child hunger crisis
content.standfirst: Premature twins arrived at an Aden hospital severely malnourished after their family fled fighting on foot. The UN says aid has been cut off for hundreds of thousands as renewed conflict drives displacement and prices higher.

image.caption: Children in Yemen face homelessness and malnutrition as fighting continues.

sources.originalTitle: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis

segments.body: Seven-week-old twins Raghad and Raad were diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition after their family fled fighting in south-west Yemen and travelled for three days on foot to Aden. Their father told the BBC that war had pushed up the price of baby milk; at times he could give the children only water.

segments.title: Hospitals under strain
segments.body: At al-Sadaqah hospital, staff said limited funding, equipment and beds meant that only the most critical patients could be admitted. The UN says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced since an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer. The agency says civilians in Taiz are at grave risk and facing food shortages.

content.headline: UK urges households to keep three days of emergency supplies
content.shortHeadline: UK campaign urges households to prepare for 72 hours
content.standfirst: The government’s Be Ready campaign advises people to store water, food and basic essentials against severe weather, cyber incidents and other emergencies. Ministers say household preparation should support wider national resilience.

image.caption: UK guidance advises households to keep essential supplies for three days.

sources.originalTitle: Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises
Five things you should do in a ‘doomsday scenario’ as UK’s disaster plan revealed

segments.body: The government is advising households to keep enough supplies to manage for 72 hours during a serious emergency, including nine litres of drinking water per person and three days’ worth of food. The guidance also recommends blankets, cash, a first-aid kit, a torch with batteries and a wind-up radio.

segments.title: Preparedness beyond the household
segments.body: The Cabinet Office campaign asks people to plan with neighbours and consider extra support for those who may need help. The government says people can build supplies gradually and should check them regularly. Ministers link the advice to risks including severe weather, disruption to services and hostile-state activity; the guidance is part of a three-year public information campaign.

content.headline: UK plans AI wildfire unit and £45m for firefighters’ protective gear
content.shortHeadline: UK plans AI wildfire unit and £45m for fire crews
content.standfirst: At a wildfire resilience summit, ministers are due to set out plans for faster fire detection, specialist equipment and military aircraft to support crews. The package follows a summer of severe fires and warnings about gaps in protective gear.

image.caption: Firefighters inspect scorched scrubland near Dunwich Heath in Suffolk after a major wildfire.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham to reveal plans for AI unit to tackle wildfires after scorching summer

segments.body: The government is set to announce an AI unit in the National Situation Centre to help spot and respond to wildfires, alongside £45m for specialist protective equipment for fire crews. The plans come after a record-breaking hot summer in the UK, when prolonged dry conditions fuelled major fires.

segments.title: Support and prevention
segments.body: Ministers also plan to make military aircraft available to reach remote fires and provide £25m to restore dried-out peatlands in England, alongside grants to help farmers make landscapes more fire-resistant. The Guardian reported that more than half of 29 fire services responding to its inquiry lacked wildfire-specific protective equipment; standard gear may not protect crews from dangerous gases in smoke.

content.headline: Children in England face some of the NHS’s longest waits, report finds
content.shortHeadline: NHS waits leave 80,000 children waiting over a year
content.standfirst: A Care Quality Commission report says 80,000 children and young people have waited more than a year for community health appointments. Delays can worsen conditions, while access and outcomes vary widely by region.

image.caption: Children face longer waits for treatment as demand rises and staff numbers fall.

sources.originalTitle: Child health in England at risk from sharp rise in NHS waiting times, report says

segments.body: Around 80,000 children and young people in England have been waiting more than a year for an appointment in community health services—almost 11 times the number of adults, according to the Care Quality Commission’s annual report. The CQC says children are among those hit hardest by rising demand and falling staff numbers.

segments.title: Uneven access
segments.body: The report warns that children’s conditions can worsen and become harder to treat while they wait. It also highlights regional differences in access, outcomes and rates of hospital admissions for conditions including diabetes and asthma. The Department of Health and Social Care says the report shows the scale of the challenge and points to plans to improve care.

content.headline: Kerosene leak continues to trouble River Taff residents and wildlife
content.shortHeadline: Kerosene pollution raises concerns along River Taff
content.standfirst: Residents reported strong odours and irritation after thousands of litres of kerosene entered the Welsh river. Natural Resources Wales says its investigation is continuing and that fuel already in drainage pipes may still reach the water.

image.caption: Health officials advised people to stay away from affected parts of the River Taff.

sources.originalTitle: Unsafe water, burning eyes and kerosene slicks: residents demand answers on River Taff leak

segments.body: Kerosene from a GE Aerospace site in Nantgarw entered the River Taff after a breach identified on 16 October. Natural Resources Wales said about four kilometres of waterway were affected, but it could not confirm how much fuel entered the river. People living nearby were advised to avoid contaminated areas and keep windows and doors shut.

segments.title: Investigation and impact
segments.body: Residents told the Guardian that fumes caused burning eyes and headaches; a local farm said it could no longer safely use river-access grazing areas. A Cardiff University water researcher warned that kerosene could harm aquatic life and birds. NRW says containment measures are in place, its investigation is ongoing and fuel left in the drainage network may still flow into the river. GE Aerospace says the source was isolated and clean-up is continuing.

content.headline: Migration settlement plans deepen Labour tensions after union talks collapse
content.shortHeadline: Union talks collapse as Labour splits over migration plans
content.standfirst: Unison says a meeting with Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood was cancelled after it sought to bring an affected care worker. Ministers are consulting on changes to settlement rules, while Labour figures disagree over how the plans should apply.

sources.originalTitle: Mahmood migration talks axed after union demands care worker joins private meeting
Minister insists she backs migration policy after joking she couldn’t lie about supporting it

segments.body: A meeting between Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and Unison general secretary Andrea Egan did not take place after Unison sought to bring a migrant care worker who would be affected by the proposed settlement changes. Unison blames the Home Secretary for refusing the request; a Home Office source says the union chose to cancel a meeting intended to be private.

segments.title: Disagreement over the proposals
segments.body: The proposals have prompted opposition from Unison and Labour MPs, who warn that longer waits could affect workers already in the UK, including in social care. The accounts describe the proposed timetable differently: one says the default wait could rise from five to 15 years, while another describes a five-to-10-year extension, with some people waiting longer. The government says it is considering consultation responses before deciding the final arrangements.

content.headline: PHP security flaw prompts emergency fixes as exploit attempts multiply
content.shortHeadline: PHP flaw triggers emergency fixes and millions of probes
content.standfirst: The vulnerability has prompted government services and companies to take websites offline while applying fixes. Security firms report a sharp rise in attempts to exploit it, but there are no confirmed successful attacks in the reporting.

image.caption: A BBC webpage was temporarily unavailable during the PHP security response.

sources.originalTitle: Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found

segments.body: A serious vulnerability in PHP, a programming language used by a large share of websites, has led organisations to take systems offline and apply security updates. In the UK, 32 government services were unavailable and four partly unavailable, ministers told Parliament; the government said no large public-facing critical service had been affected.

segments.title: The scale of the risk is still unclear
segments.body: Cloudflare’s chief executive reported millions of attempts to exploit the flaw after it became public, while Amazon said it had also seen attempts. The National Cyber Security Centre said it had no reports of successful hacks as a result of the vulnerability; the BBC reported that the effects may take time to become clear. Some older systems may need replacement rather than a straightforward patch.

content.headline: New Telford factory restarts UK production of tank gun barrels
content.shortHeadline: Telford factory brings tank barrel production back to UK
content.standfirst: A Rheinmetall plant has begun making artillery barrels in Shropshire, restoring a capability the UK has lacked for decades. The factory is part of a wider European effort to expand defence production after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

image.caption: Wes Streeting inspects equipment used to produce large-calibre weapons at the Telford factory.

sources.originalTitle: Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK

segments.body: The UK defence secretary opened a Rheinmetall factory in Telford where production of artillery barrels has begun. The company says the plant can make 245 barrels a year, with capacity to expand if orders allow. It is expected to produce for German-made howitzers first, with British tank barrels also possible in future.

segments.title: A push to produce at scale
segments.body: The factory follows a rapid investment decision made before a formal contract was in place. The army’s chief of the general staff said artillery remains essential despite the focus on drone warfare, arguing that drones cannot match its firepower. Rheinmetall says the barrels are designed to withstand substantially more firing than Russian equivalents; that comparison is the company’s claim.

content.headline: Russia’s activity near undersea cables raises concern over UK naval capacity
content.shortHeadline: Russian activity renews concern over UK undersea cables
content.standfirst: An investigation cited by the i Paper found more than 500 instances of Russian civilian vessels near vital cables in four and a half years. Experts warn that the Royal Navy is stretched, while the government says it is monitoring activity and investing in protection.

image.caption: The Royal Navy has reported Russian submarine activity near undersea cables and pipelines.

sources.originalTitle: Putin has become increasingly brazen at sea. Where the UK is vulnerable

segments.body: More than 500 instances of Russian civilian vessels loitering over vital undersea cables were identified in an investigation reported by the i Paper. The activity could indicate that vessels are mapping infrastructure, but the report does not establish that the cables have been damaged. Undersea cables carry data essential to communications, public services and financial transactions.

segments.title: Security and readiness
segments.body: Defence experts cited in the report say the Royal Navy is under pressure, including gaps in its ability to operate beneath Arctic ice and shortages of submarine commanders. The Ministry of Defence says the Navy monitors Russian activity and has worked with cable operators; it also points to investment in surveillance ships and £330m for protecting critical underwater infrastructure.

content.headline: Leaked Novo Nordisk list ranks nearly 7,000 Danish health professionals
content.shortHeadline: Leaked list ranks 7,000 Danish health professionals for Novo
content.standfirst: Material attributed to a hacker group appears to rank doctors and nurses by commercial value and loyalty to the company’s medicines. Novo Nordisk says it has not verified the material; a doctor listed says she never consented to being included.

sources.originalTitle: Datalæk fra hackerangreb: Novo rangerer tusindvis af sundhedspersoner fra A til D

segments.body: A leaked document reported by Ingeniøren and reviewed in part by DR appears to rank nearly 7,000 Danish doctors and nurses from A to D according to their commercial value to Novo Nordisk and their loyalty to its products. The material is said to have come from a hacker group that claimed to have copied data from the company.

segments.title: Company and professionals respond
segments.body: Novo Nordisk says it has not verified the material because it may have been obtained through criminal activity, and says it is normal for pharmaceutical companies to use databases of health professionals. A doctors’ representative says she never gave consent to being listed and is concerned about the detail recorded. The industry association says it expects people on such lists to have consented, but could not explain why this doctor was included.

content.headline: Danish minister calls for plan to replace outdated critical IT systems
content.shortHeadline: Denmark plans digital recovery effort for outdated IT
content.standfirst: Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen says parts of Denmark’s digital infrastructure rely on old systems that need replacing. The proposal follows recent cyber incidents and earlier audits that found weaknesses in public-sector IT preparedness.

image.caption: Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen says outdated systems in critical areas need to be replaced.

sources.originalTitle: IT-sikkerhed udfordret: Minister varsler digital genopretningsplan

segments.body: Denmark needs a recovery plan for its digital resilience, Minister for Societal Security and Emergency Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen has told Politiken. She says outdated IT systems in critical areas should be replaced, but has not identified them, saying greater detail could create a security risk.

segments.title: Longstanding preparedness gaps
segments.body: The minister’s proposal follows recent digital attacks, including a breach involving names, addresses and CPR numbers of about 8.8 million people, according to the report. Earlier audits by the National Audit Office found inadequate IT emergency preparedness in seven of 12 systems examined in 2023, after finding deficiencies in all 13 systems in a previous review.

content.headline: Personalised melanoma vaccine cuts recurrence risk in a large trial
content.shortHeadline: Trial finds personalised melanoma vaccine lowers recurrence risk
content.standfirst: In a trial of more than 1,100 patients, a personalised mRNA vaccine alongside Keytruda reduced the reported risk of recurrence or death by 42% compared with Keytruda alone. The vaccine is not approved, and longer-term results are pending.

image.caption: A personalised mRNA vaccine is being studied as an addition to Keytruda after melanoma surgery.

sources.originalTitle: Skræddersyet vaccine kan blive nyt våben mod modermærkekræft

segments.body: A phase 3 trial of more than 1,100 people with high-risk melanoma found that a personalised mRNA vaccine combined with Keytruda was associated with a 42% lower risk of recurrence or death than Keytruda alone, according to results released by Moderna and Merck. At two years, 82.2% of the vaccine group were alive without recurrence, compared with 70% of the comparison group.

segments.title: Further evidence needed
segments.body: The vaccine is designed around mutations in an individual patient’s tumour and is intended to train the immune system to recognise cancer cells. Researchers are continuing to follow trial participants to assess longer-term outcomes. The treatment has not yet been approved; the companies are preparing an application in the United States.

content.headline: UN climate report raises projected warming to 2.7C under current pledges
content.shortHeadline: Climate pledges now point to 2.7C of warming, UN says
content.standfirst: The UN Environment Programme’s estimate rises from 2.5C, assuming countries deliver their existing plans. The report says emissions must fall much faster to limit the overshoot above 1.5C.

image.caption: Donald Trump has backed increased US fossil-fuel production as global warming projections worsen.

sources.originalTitle: Nu rammer Trumps 'drill baby, drill' for alvor klimaets kongetal

segments.body: The UN Environment Programme now projects about 2.7C of warming by the end of the century if countries implement their current climate plans, up from an estimate of 2.5C in the previous assessment. The report says the world is on course to exceed the Paris agreement’s 1.5C ambition.

segments.title: A steeper emissions decline required
segments.body: The report says limiting the overshoot to the lowest feasible range of 1.7C to 1.8C would require global emissions to fall sharply by 2030 and continue declining through 2040. Its assessment links the worsening projection in part to the United States’ departure from the Paris agreement and rising emissions. The figures depend on countries delivering the plans they have pledged.

content.headline: European Parliament votes to delay methane rules for industry by three years
content.shortHeadline: EU methane rules delayed by three years in Parliament vote
content.standfirst: MEPs backed a longer postponement of requirements for energy imports and producers to document methane emissions. The proposal still needs EU member-state approval and has drawn criticism from climate groups.

image.caption: MEPs voted to postpone parts of the EU methane rules by three years.

sources.originalTitle: EU-parlamentarikere vil udskyde klimakrav: 'Andre hensyn end klima er rykket op på dagsordenen'

segments.body: The European Parliament has voted to delay by three years rules requiring importers and producers to document methane emissions from energy supplies. Requirements originally due to take effect in 2027 would move to 2030 under the proposal, which goes further than the one-year delay proposed by the European Commission.

segments.title: Energy security and climate concerns
segments.body: Gas-exporting countries including the United States and Qatar had warned that stricter requirements could affect exports to Europe. A coalition of more than 50 organisations says postponing the rules will not resolve energy-security concerns. The Parliament’s proposal exempts requirements applying to sanctioned countries; EU member states must still decide whether to approve the delay.

content.headline: Only 39% of Danes have prepared for a three-day emergency, DR reports
content.shortHeadline: Just 39% of Danes have three-day emergency supplies
content.standfirst: A DR report says fewer than four in 10 people have followed the authorities’ advice to keep supplies for three days. One Kolding resident describes how he built up food, water and backup power over time.

image.caption: Ulrick Göning keeps a generator in his garage for use during a crisis.

sources.originalTitle: Ulrick har preppet siden dag et: Det er ’noget sjusk’, hvis man ikke forbereder sig

segments.body: Only 39% of Danes have followed the authorities’ recommendation to keep enough supplies to manage for three days during a crisis, according to the DR report. More than half have not stocked up for a situation such as a power cut or interruption to the water supply.

Kolding resident Ulrick Göning says he began preparing three years ago and now keeps food and water at home and a generator in his garage. The authorities’ checklist was published about two years ago; Göning says households able to do so should follow its advice and maintain their supplies.

content.headline: Bournemouth's 3-0 win over Milan underlines Premier League's European power
content.shortHeadline: Bournemouth beat Milan 3-0 as Premier League power shows
content.standfirst: Bournemouth beat seven-time European champions AC Milan in only their third European fixture. The result also feeds a broader picture of English clubs' strength in the Europa League and Conference League.

image.caption: Bournemouth have beaten Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz and AC Milan in the Europa League.

sources.originalTitle: Dream night for Bournemouth - win over Milan a sign of Premier League power

segments.body: Justin Kluivert opened the scoring as Bournemouth beat AC Milan 3-0 at Vitality Stadium. Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan was sent off after 27 minutes, but BBC Sport reports Bournemouth were the better side even before the dismissal.

segments.title: A wider English advantage
segments.body: The report places the win in the context of Premier League clubs' strong recent record in Europe's secondary competitions: English sides have lost just four of 26 continental matches this season. It points to greater broadcasting income, spending and wages as key advantages, while noting that this success has not translated into consistent Champions League wins.

content.headline: Brook's record 202 cannot prevent Sri Lanka's remarkable 430 chase
content.shortHeadline: Brook's record 202 ends in defeat as Sri Lanka chase 430
content.standfirst: Harry Brook made England's first ODI double-century, but Sri Lanka completed the second-highest successful chase in the format's history. England now need to win their next two matches to reach the tri-series final.

image.caption: Harry Brook hit the fastest double-century in ODI history.

sources.originalTitle: Sri Lanka make 430 to beat England after Brook's 202
Brook underlines status as world's best all-format batter in remarkable defeat

segments.body: Brook struck 202 from 116 balls as England made 429-4 in Rawalpindi, but Sri Lanka reached 430-8 with one ball to spare. Pavan Rathnayake made 130, while Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka each scored 97. It was the second-highest successful chase in men's ODI history.

segments.title: A record innings, a costly defeat
segments.body: England's bowling and fielding faltered in difficult conditions. Sam Curran conceded 103 runs from nine overs, and the report questions the use of the bowling options as Sri Lanka kept pace with the target. England have no wins after two tri-series matches and need to beat Pakistan in their next two games to reach the final.

perspectives.body: BBC cricket correspondent Stephan Shemilt argues that the innings further establishes Brook as a leading all-format batter. He also highlights the demands of Brook's workload and the absence of a major tournament win to match his individual milestones.

content.headline: South Africa rout Australia to level series and raise selection questions
content.shortHeadline: South Africa level series after innings win over Australia
content.standfirst: South Africa won the second Test by an innings and 31 runs, levelling the series with one match left. Australia's batting failures have put several places under scrutiny ahead of the decider.

image.caption: Australia were beaten by an innings and 31 runs in Gqeberha.

sources.originalTitle: What next for Australia after chastening defeat by South Africa?

segments.body: Australia were bowled out for 99 in their first innings and made 295 in their second, with Travis Head scoring 121. South Africa's 425-9 declared secured an innings-and-31-run win in Gqeberha and wiped out Australia's series lead.

segments.title: Selection under pressure
segments.body: Marnus Labuschagne has gone 47 innings without an international century, while opener Nic Maddinson's three low scores in the series have left his place in doubt. Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis and Cooper Connolly are among the possible options discussed in the report. The series decider begins in Cape Town on Tuesday.

content.headline: Manchester United keep Fernandes as captain amid Carrick uncertainty
content.shortHeadline: Fernandes stays captain as United weigh Carrick's future
content.standfirst: Bruno Fernandes will not be disciplined for criticising Michael Carrick after Manchester United's 4-1 loss to Como. Carrick is expected to lead Sunday's match, but the club has begun identifying possible replacements.

image.caption: Michael Carrick apologises to Manchester United's 700 travelling fans after the defeat by Como.

sources.originalTitle: Fernandes to stay captain as Rooney calls Man Utd players babies
Carrick carrying on but senior Man Utd figures concerned by performances

segments.body: Fernandes remains Manchester United captain after questioning Carrick's tactics following the defeat by Como. The club will not discipline him. Carrick is expected to be in charge against Bournemouth on Sunday, although senior figures are concerned about results and performances.

segments.title: Responsibility under debate
segments.body: United have begun identifying possible replacements, but some at the club believe frequent managerial changes have not solved the team's decline and that underperforming players also bear responsibility. Former United striker Wayne Rooney, speaking on the United Stand podcast, called the players selfish and said they needed to take responsibility on the pitch.

perspectives.body: Rooney says Fernandes and other players risk shifting blame away from their own performances. He also urged the club's board to clarify Carrick's position and advised the head coach to stand up for himself.

content.headline: Celtic's European collapse deepens with third straight Europa League loss
content.shortHeadline: Celtic lose third straight Europa League game
content.standfirst: Celtic led Celta Vigo before conceding twice in three minutes to lose 2-1. They are 35th of 36 teams after three Europa League defeats, and criticism is growing over their ability to compete at this level.

sources.originalTitle: O'Neill bemoans marginal moments but are Celtic just not good enough?

segments.body: Mika Baur put Celtic ahead on 47 minutes, but Javi Rodriguez scored twice in three minutes as Celta Vigo won 2-1. Celtic have now lost all three of their Europa League matches and sit 35th in the 36-team table.

segments.title: Questions after another collapse
segments.body: Manager Martin O'Neill pointed to a free-kick decision and a missed chance to make it 2-0. Former Scotland attacker James McFadden said Celtic were short of the required standard, while former Celtic goalkeeper Pat Bonner questioned whether they were good enough individually and collectively. O'Neill said his side must find a way to win their remaining European games.

content.headline: Counties interested in signing James Anderson after Lancashire exit
content.shortHeadline: Counties ready to speak to Anderson after Lancashire exit
content.standfirst: Several counties are interested in speaking to James Anderson if he wants to continue playing next summer. The 44-year-old must decide whether to retire or leave Lancashire, where he took 50 Championship wickets last season.

image.caption: James Anderson first played for Lancashire's first team in 2001.

sources.originalTitle: Counties interested in Anderson after Lancs exit

segments.body: Lancashire will not offer Anderson a new contract, ending his playing association with the county where he made his first-team debut in 2001. Clubs in both divisions of the County Championship are interested, and some have already approached him. Anderson had planned to play for another year.

segments.title: A decision still to come
segments.body: Anderson took 50 wickets in Division Two last summer and was Lancashire's County Championship player of the year. Any move may depend on finances, the role offered and the time required away from his home. Whether he continues as a player or retires is not yet known.

content.headline: Ruti Aga receives six-year ban after fake prescription claim
content.shortHeadline: Ruti Aga handed six-year ban for doping and tampering
content.standfirst: The Ethiopian marathon runner tested positive for a prohibited steroid after winning a half-marathon in China. She received a further four-year ban after investigators found the prescription she submitted came from a non-existent clinic.

image.caption: Ruti Aga won the 2019 Tokyo Marathon.

sources.originalTitle: Aga banned for fake prescription from family member

segments.body: Ruti Aga has been banned for six years after testing positive for methylprednisolone and then misleading investigators. The Athletics Integrity Unit said the 32-year-old submitted a prescription from a clinic that did not exist, issued by a family member who was not medically registered. The ban runs from her provisional suspension on 10 September.

content.headline: US to host first Women's Club World Cup in 2028, with Arsenal named
content.shortHeadline: US to host inaugural Women's Club World Cup in 2028
content.standfirst: Fifa has confirmed the United States as host of the first Women's Club World Cup, scheduled for January 2028. Arsenal are among seven clubs already named for the 19-team tournament.

image.caption: The United States will host the first Women's Club World Cup in 2028.

sources.originalTitle: US to host first Women's Club World Cup in 2028

segments.body: The inaugural Women's Club World Cup will run from 5 to 30 January 2028 in the United States. Arsenal, Barcelona, Gotham, Club America, Corinthians, Naegohyang and Wuhan Jiangda have been named; the other 12 places are yet to be determined.

segments.title: A scheduling concern
segments.body: The competition is planned as a 19-team event held every four years. The Women's Super League has previously described its mid-season scheduling as potentially "catastrophic", amid broader concerns about the demands of the women's football calendar.

content.headline: Leonard Cohen’s greatest songs, ranked: heartbreak, hope and imperfection
content.shortHeadline: Leonard Cohen’s greatest songs, ranked
content.standfirst: A decade after Cohen’s final album and his death, a ranking revisits songs that turn love, grief, faith and mortality into sharply observed, often wry reflections on being human.

image.caption: Leonard Cohen.

sources.originalTitle: Heartbreak, hope and human imperfection: Leonard Cohen’s greatest songs – ranked!

segments.body: The ranking makes a case for Cohen’s range: from the menace of “First We Take Manhattan” to the mordant humour of “Everybody Knows” and the late-life poise of “You Want It Darker”. It argues that his best songs hold sorrow and wit together rather than settling for a single, definitive mood.

segments.title: The songs that keep opening up
segments.body: “Famous Blue Raincoat” is singled out for its shadowy, intimate portrait of a love triangle, while “Anthem” offers hope without denying imperfection. The list is candid about its limits, too: choosing 20 songs means leaving out plenty of worthy work, and its order reflects personal judgement rather than an uncontested ranking.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse tribute show struggles to escape the memory of its original
content.shortHeadline: An Amy Winehouse tribute struggles to match the original
content.standfirst: The Roundhouse concert revisits Back to Black for its 20th anniversary, with Jorja Smith and other singers taking on Winehouse’s songs. A review finds the most convincing moments come when the performers make the material their own.

image.caption: Jorja Smith performs at the Back to Black 20 anniversary concert at the Roundhouse in London.

sources.originalTitle: Amy Winehouse: Back to Black 20 review – trying an all-star Amy tribute show is a losing game

segments.body: The Amy Winehouse Band’s precision and gusto cannot replace the qualities the review hears in Winehouse herself: her playfulness, bite and unruly charisma. The anniversary show recreates Back to Black with singers including Jorja Smith, Lianne La Havas and Corinne Bailey Rae, but its television staging interrupts the album’s flow with interviews and introductions.

segments.title: Where the tribute finds its own voice
segments.body: The performances come alive when they move beyond imitation. Jessie Reyez brings conviction to “Rehab”, Flo rework “He Can Only Hold Her”, and Yebba gives “Love Is a Losing Game” a spare, spectral arrangement. The ensemble finale of “Valerie” offers a rare moment of joyful disorder, leaving the show with a warm glow even as the review argues that Winehouse’s own intensity remains unmatched.

content.headline: Shovel Dance Collective turns English folk into ecstatic, dissonant noise
content.shortHeadline: Shovel Dance Collective makes folk music feel unruly and new
content.standfirst: On Everything in Readiness, the nine-piece London group sends traditional songs through drones, distortion and abrupt sonic shifts. The review hears both a thrillingly original sound and an argument for folk’s continuing relevance.

image.caption: Shovel Dance Collective.

sources.originalTitle: Shovel Dance Collective: Everything in Readiness review – ecstatic, dissonant folk music fighting for sonic and spiritual freedom

segments.body: Everything in Readiness opens with a long, shifting suite and moves from tape hiss and unaccompanied singing to distorted guitar and surging noise. The review describes a record that refuses to ease listeners in, but finds its disorientation part of the point: centuries-old material becomes strange and immediate again.

segments.title: A turbulent history, heard anew
segments.body: The band’s politics inform its choices of material, including “Bold Captain Avery”, which recasts a 17th-century celebration of a pirate whose real violence sits uneasily beneath the song’s heroic image. The review sees the group drawing contemporary connections from a turbulent past, while arguing that the album’s head-spinning sound is its most immediate pleasure.

content.headline: Country singer John Anderson, known for ‘Swingin’’, dies aged 71
content.shortHeadline: Country singer John Anderson dies aged 71
content.standfirst: The Florida-born singer-songwriter had five country chart-toppers and a career spanning nearly five decades. His family announced his death; Anderson was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024.

image.caption: John Anderson performs in Nashville in 2024.

sources.originalTitle: John Anderson, five-time US country chart-topper, dies aged 71

segments.body: John Anderson, a traditionalist country singer whose hits included “Swingin’”, “Seminole Wind” and “Straight Tequila Night”, has died aged 71. His family announced the news on social media, remembering him not only as a musician whose songs touched many lives, but as the heart of their family.

segments.title: A long road through country music
segments.body: Anderson went to Nashville after high school, working manual jobs while pursuing music. His breakthrough came in the late 1970s, followed by chart success with songs including “Wild and Blue” and “Black Sheep”. After a difficult stretch between record labels, he returned to prominence with 1992’s Seminole Wind and continued recording and performing after serious illness.

content.headline: Jason Molina’s friends recall the restless imagination behind his songs
content.shortHeadline: Remembering Jason Molina’s music and restless imagination
content.standfirst: A new documentary revisits the life of the Songs: Ohia and Magnolia Electric Co songwriter. Friends and collaborators describe his prolific work, vivid storytelling and the alcoholism that contributed to his death at 39.

image.caption: Jason Molina performs as the Magnolia Electric Co at All Tomorrow’s Parties in 2007.

sources.originalTitle: ‘He had this electrical charge’: the short life and long legacy of Jason Molina, master of Americana

segments.body: Jason Molina grew up in industrial Lorain, Ohio, a place of economic decline that became a recurring presence in his songs. He released almost 20 studio albums and numerous EPs, moving between lo-fi recordings, slowcore and Americana before his death in 2013, aged 39, after years of alcoholism.

segments.title: Songs that made their own world
segments.body: Friends describe an unusually energetic, generous musician whose stories blurred fact and invention. His songs carried that quality into a private imaginative world of recurring images, ghosts and hauntings. The documentary also traces the making of 2003’s The Magnolia Electric Co, which collaborators recall as a striking leap in scale and a moment when the songs felt timeless.

segments.title: A legacy still finding listeners
segments.body: Molina’s audience has grown since his death, with younger artists including Phoebe Bridgers, MJ Lenderman and Waxahatchee among those cited as admirers. The film’s director, Tommy Nickoloff, says making it was a way to help more people discover Molina’s work and life; the article also recounts the later years when alcoholism increasingly disrupted his touring and music-making.

content.headline: Cyndi Lauper’s auction looks back on a career built on creative freedom
content.shortHeadline: Cyndi Lauper puts a lifetime of style and music on view
content.standfirst: As Lauper auctions outfits, memorabilia and personal items, she reflects on the individuality behind her 1980s image, her advocacy work and the freedom she hopes younger artists will claim.

image.caption: Cyndi Lauper among pieces from her career collection.

sources.originalTitle: Cyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’

segments.body: Cyndi Lauper’s two-part Bonhams auction gathers clothes and objects from a five-decade career, from the leopard-print pyjamas worn in “Girls Just Want to Have Fun” to handwritten lyrics and the newspaper skirt from her True Colors artwork. Lauper says she hopes the collection will prompt older fans to remember creative individuality and younger ones to discover it.

segments.title: Style as self-expression
segments.body: Lauper traces her inventive style to growing up in Queens and working at Manhattan vintage shop Screaming Mimi’s before fame. She describes the freedom of the 1980s as a contrast with what she calls a more corporatised culture, and points to Chappell Roan’s writing and visual choices as examples of creativity she relates to now.

segments.title: Joy, advocacy and disagreement
segments.body: Lauper discusses her work supporting homeless LGBTQ+ youth and her belief that dialogue matters more than cancellation. Asked about Nicki Minaj’s later political associations, she says she does not regret collaborating: she views the song’s message of women claiming joy as political in itself, while acknowledging that she does not know what Minaj is doing now.

content.headline: Fontaines DC’s early Dublin shows hinted at their stadium-sized rise
content.shortHeadline: How Fontaines DC grew from Dublin students to stadium headliners
content.standfirst: People who encountered the band in its early Dublin years recall the ambition and restless songwriting that preceded its rise. The story also returns to the venues, neighbourhoods and local figures that shaped the group’s beginnings.

image.caption: Fontaines DC perform at Finsbury Park.

sources.originalTitle: The breathtaking rise of Fontaines DC, by the people who were there

segments.body: In 2018, Fontaines DC were still a support act at Dublin’s Tivoli Theatre. Eight years later, with a fifth album released and stadium shows ahead, the band’s growth looks striking. Early supporters recall that even small gigs carried a sense of purpose: the group wanted to write better songs and move beyond the local post-punk scene.

segments.title: A band formed in a city of outsiders
segments.body: The members met through the British and Irish Modern Music Institute in Dublin, despite coming from different parts of Ireland and Spain. Their early songs drew on the city they inhabited—its streets, pubs and pressures—while their literary interests were genuine, the feature argues, rather than simply a marketable image.

segments.title: From local momentum to a wider audience
segments.body: Teachers and promoters describe a band that built its following through rehearsal, new songs and increasingly ambitious bookings. The article remembers local promoter Trevor Dietz, who died last year, as an early advocate, and traces how the band’s profile grew beyond Ireland during the pandemic era.

content.headline: Madness look back on their early years in restored film Take It or Leave It
content.shortHeadline: Madness revisit their early years in Take It or Leave It
content.standfirst: A restored 4K version of the band’s 1981 film follows its members from dead-end jobs to chart success. Suggs and Mark Bedford recall why they wanted an improvised, funny and unusually grounded account of starting a band.

image.caption: Madness in the restored film Take It or Leave It.

sources.originalTitle: Suggs from Madness: ‘Middle-class bands didn’t put the time in like we did’

segments.body: Take It or Leave It, newly restored by the BFI, follows Madness’s early days through a mix of black-and-white and colour scenes. Rather than a conventional rock-star fantasy, the band and director Dave Robinson aimed for something closer to lived experience, with scenes based on interviews and dialogue improvised from the musicians’ memories.

segments.title: The work behind the jokes
segments.body: Suggs recalls the band’s jobs, rehearsals and setbacks, including his own temporary dismissal after skipping out to watch Chelsea. The film’s humour drew on shared interests in British comedy, but the band also wanted to show the discipline behind its success. For Bedford, the lasting point was simpler: making music that gives people pleasure.

content.headline: Ali G sequel sparks anger from a Republican recruit as review questions its bite
content.shortHeadline: Ali G sequel draws a lawsuit threat and a mixed review
content.standfirst: A Republican county party chair says he plans to sue over footage used in Ali G: Who Iz I? The Guardian review finds the sequel’s deliberately crude pranks sometimes funny, but questions whether its targets and format still land.

image.caption: Sacha Baron Cohen at the world premiere of Ali G: Who Iz I?

sources.originalTitle: Ali G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad taste
Republican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’

segments.body: Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G: Who Iz I? returns to the character’s prank-based comedy, mixing hoaxes with the fictional Erran Morad and a new, self-righteous liberal character. The review describes a deliberately bad-taste film that takes aim in multiple directions, but says it does not land a major blow on a prominent target in the way the Borat sequel did.

segments.title: A participant says he was misled
segments.body: The chair of the El Paso County Republican Party, Michael Aboud, says he believed he was taking part in a documentary about immigration and self-defence training. After seeing footage used in the film, he called Baron Cohen and the crew liars and said he planned to sue. Aboud declined to comment when asked whether he stood by his actions shown in the film. Representatives told the Guardian that another participant, Joshua Loudermilk, was unaware of the film’s true nature.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s reporting highlights a dispute about what Aboud understood he was filming. The article says he did not know his participation was in a comedy film until the newspaper contacted him; his stated intention to sue is not a legal finding.

content.headline: Wicker’s unusual romantic lead taps into a conversation about care and desire
content.shortHeadline: Why audiences are falling for Wicker’s basket-made husband
content.standfirst: The romantic fantasy pairs Olivia Colman’s ostracised fisherwoman with a husband woven from wicker. Its creators and cultural commentators say the online fascination reaches beyond the outlandish premise to questions of domestic work, desire and who gets to be considered attractive.

image.caption: The wicker-husband fantasy Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker

segments.body: In Wicker, a fisherwoman commissions a basketmaker to weave her a husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård. The trailer prompted a wave of online jokes and thirst, including a popcorn bucket designed from a scan of the actor’s torso. The filmmakers say the husband’s appeal is not only his looks: he notices what needs doing at home and does it without expecting praise.

segments.title: A fantasy with familiar tensions
segments.body: The film-makers say the story, adapted from Ursula Wills-Jones’s short story, speaks to the unequal domestic workload many couples still negotiate. The Fisherwoman is an autonomous outsider who seeks out a partner, rather than a heroine trapped into a romance. Commentators connect the film to a wider genre of human-monster romances that explores desire, difference and social expectations.

content.headline: Ramla Ali’s journey from refugee to Olympian reaches the screen in In the0Shad…
content.shortHeadline: Ramla Ali’s journey from refugee to Olympian becomes a film
content.standfirst: In the Shadows dramatises the boxer’s path from fleeing Somalia to competing at the Tokyo Olympics. Ali and actor Jasmine Jobson discuss the family history behind the film and the risks of telling a story that is both personal and political.

image.caption: Jasmine Jobson and Ramla Ali at the London premiere of In the Shadows.

sources.originalTitle: ‘If my brother hadn’t died, my life would be so different’: Olympic boxer Ramla Ali’s incredible journey

segments.body: Ramla Ali was born in Somalia; after her older brother was killed in an explosion, her family fled the civil war and arrived in the UK as refugees. She began boxing in east London while keeping it from her family. In the Shadows, starring Jasmine Jobson, follows Ali’s journey to the 2021 Tokyo Olympics, where she became the first boxer to represent Somalia.

segments.title: A family story on screen
segments.body: Ali says she worried about exposing private family experiences, but her mother wanted the scene of her brother’s death included. Ali describes that loss as the event that changed the family’s path. She also hopes audiences leave seeing a person rather than a headline about migration, and says she wants to make more films focused on Black British experiences.

segments.title: Taking on the role
segments.body: Jobson says she had two weeks to prepare for the boxing scenes and worked to make the portrayal authentic to Ali. She describes similarities in their determination while stressing that their life experiences were not the same. Ali was involved in the production, reviewing script drafts and spending time on set.

content.headline: Taika Waititi and Kazuo Ishiguro debate the changes in Klara and the Sun
content.shortHeadline: Klara and the Sun’s creators discuss adaptation, love and AI
content.standfirst: Waititi’s film adaptation of Ishiguro’s novel has divided critics while winning over some younger festival-goers. Their conversation explores what changes when a spare story about an artificial friend reaches the screen—and what its author says it is not about.

image.caption: Jenna Ortega as Klara in Klara and the Sun.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the Sun

segments.body: Taika Waititi’s adaptation stars Jenna Ortega as Klara, a solar-powered artificial friend to a sick teenager. The Guardian’s critic is less persuaded by the film than by Ishiguro’s spare novel, finding that comic flourishes and pratfalls do not always fit its parts together. The film has nevertheless been a favourite among some young influencers at the festival.

segments.title: Adaptation and emotional complexity
segments.body: Ishiguro argues that a film should use its imagination rather than simply reproduce a book, and Waititi agrees that adaptation should bring original ideas. Both describe the story as concerned with loneliness and the complexity of love, as well as the prospect of death and the human willingness to adapt to loss.

segments.title: A story, not an AI handbook
segments.body: Ishiguro says he was unaware that a Google DeepMind executive had cited the novel as a possible ethical touchstone for AI development. He cautions that the story was not written to guide the industry and may not be a good resource for those questions. Waititi answers with a joke: “The Terminator’s a good one.”

content.headline: The Social Reckoning turns Facebook’s internal files into an uneasy drama
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning dramatizes Facebook’s whistleblower story
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network centres on reporter Jeff Horwitz and whistleblower Frances Haugen. A review finds the film’s account of Facebook’s influence sobering, while questioning whether the drama has enough urgency to change viewers’ minds.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling

segments.body: The Social Reckoning follows Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, played by Jeremy Allen White, as he investigates Facebook with help from former employee Frances Haugen, played by Mikey Madison. The film draws on reporting about internal documents concerning the platform’s effects on teenage girls, political misinformation and the way its recommendation systems can push users toward extremist groups.

segments.title: The uneasy distance between screen and audience
segments.body: The review describes the film as an investigative journalism drama that borrows the fast dialogue and shifting timelines of its predecessor but adopts a darker tone. Its central question is whether the revelations can still shock an audience accustomed to ongoing concerns about social media. The critic writes that watching it felt frightening, yet found herself returning to the platforms she criticises.

content.headline: Fatherland finds personal pain beneath Thomas Mann’s postwar homecoming
content.shortHeadline: Fatherland looks beyond Thomas Mann’s public homecoming
content.standfirst: Paweł Pawlikowski’s monochrome historical drama follows the novelist’s 1949 return to divided Germany with his daughter Erika. The review sees their private grief complicating Mann’s attempt to stand above the politics of the moment.

image.caption: Sandra Hüller as Erika Mann and Hanns Zischler as Thomas Mann in Fatherland.

sources.originalTitle: Fatherland review – Sandra Hüller brings a bayonet of intelligence to Paweł Pawlikowski’s taut return

segments.body: In 1949, Thomas Mann returns to Germany from California exile, accepting an award in Frankfurt and planning another in Weimar, now in the communist East. Accompanied by his daughter Erika, played by Sandra Hüller, he tries to maintain a diplomatically ambiguous position across the country’s divided political landscape.

segments.title: A family’s grief challenges neutrality
segments.body: Erika is grieving her brother Klaus, a writer living in American exile. The review argues that Klaus’s fate unsettles the film’s portrait of Mann’s careful distance from political choices: his son’s writing and personal crisis make questions of compromise and responsibility impossible to keep at arm’s length. The film offers no easy consolation, finding only a measure of release in Bach’s music.

content.headline: The Audacity skewers Silicon Valley’s wealthy, self-serving characters
content.shortHeadline: The Audacity takes aim at Silicon Valley’s tech titans
content.standfirst: Jonathan Glatzer’s comedy-drama follows a data-company CEO surrounded by people as compromised as he is. A review praises its pace and unpleasant characters; Glatzer and cast discuss the show’s real-world echoes, from AI to children’s data.

image.caption: Billy Magnussen as Duncan Park in The Audacity.

sources.originalTitle: The Audacity review – cracking TV packed with even more gloriously awful people than Succession
‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV show

segments.body: The Audacity centres on Duncan Park, a data-brokerage CEO whose acquisition deal collapses after he leaks news to boost his share price. The Guardian review calls the series a fast, unsettling comedy-drama crowded with greed, blackmail and twists, and sees it filling some of the space left by Succession and Silicon Valley.

segments.title: A satire with real-world targets
segments.body: Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer says the series takes aim at a tech-bro culture shaped by ambition, exclusion and environmental costs. He and actors Billy Magnussen and Zach Galifianakis point to data-gathering in schools, executives’ distrust of screens for their own children and the energy demands of data centres as concerns that inform the show’s satire.

perspectives.body: Glatzer and the actors describe the series as a warning as well as entertainment, citing the risks of children’s information being collected and of AI and data systems being controlled by a small group of powerful people.

content.headline: The Experiment tests how easily the public accepts dehumanising ideas
content.shortHeadline: The Experiment puts the public in a disturbing social test
content.standfirst: Channel 4’s programme invites members of the public to tour a fictional care home for disabled people, where actors and AI-made materials reproduce Nazi ideas in updated language. The review finds the exercise deeply uncomfortable—and asks what viewers should take from it.

image.caption: Presenters Mat Fraser and Sophie Morgan watch the experiment unfold on monitors.

sources.originalTitle: The Experiment review – easily the most disturbing thing on TV

segments.body: Mat Fraser and Sophie Morgan set out to test whether members of the public can be persuaded to accept segregated institutions for disabled people in the name of savings and productivity. The visitors encounter a fictional home called Segrilife, where disabled actors portray residents and AI-made posters and corporate films give the institution a polished veneer.

segments.title: What makes the exercise difficult to watch
segments.body: The review describes a slow build of scenes in which participants discuss a disabled person’s care costs while she sits in the room. A few visitors express concern, but it takes time before one calls the place “hell on earth”. Threaded through the experiment is the history of Aktion T4, the Nazi programme that segregated and murdered disabled people.

segments.title: The question after the reveal
segments.body: The programme’s comparison between Nazi ideology and present-day rhetoric may, the review acknowledges, alienate some viewers. But the discomfort is also its point: even after participants learn the truth, the review says, it is hard to forget how readily some accepted arguments for treating disabled people as less fully human.

content.headline: Nobody Wants This finds new romantic sparks in its third season
content.shortHeadline: Nobody Wants This shifts the romantic spotlight to its siblings
content.standfirst: Noah and Joanne move in together in the hit comedy’s new season, trading first-date excitement for domestic negotiation. The review finds fresh energy in the developing bond between their siblings, Sasha and Morgan.

image.caption: Kristen Bell as Joanne and Adam Brody as Noah in Nobody Wants This.

sources.originalTitle: Nobody Wants This review – prepare to fall in love again … with a different couple

segments.body: With Noah and Joanne living together, Nobody Wants This turns from the question of whether their relationship can survive religious and family differences to the small frictions of sharing a home. The review says the stakes are lower and the old fizz has faded, though the couple’s everyday routines still provide comic moments.

segments.title: A new will-they-won’t-they
segments.body: The season’s most promising shift comes as Noah’s brother Sasha and Joanne’s sister Morgan move closer. Sasha and his wife Esther split, giving more room to his tender connection with Morgan. The review sees the supporting characters—not the central couple—as the source of the show’s renewed romantic charge.

content.headline: Ellie & Natasia returns with surreal sketches about modern life
content.shortHeadline: Ellie & Natasia’s weird comedy is back
content.standfirst: Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou return with three half-hour episodes, skewering influencers, trad-wife content and everyday absurdities. The review finds the series uneven but often brilliantly strange, and wants more of it.

image.caption: Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in the second series of Ellie & Natasia.

sources.originalTitle: Ellie & Natasia review – please give us more of this irresistibly weird comedy

segments.body: After a four-year gap, White and Demetriou return to their sketch series with three longer episodes. The review praises recurring characters such as the unsettling beauty entrepreneurs from Internet Nails, alongside new sketches that send up podcast influencers, trad-wife content and online trends.

segments.title: A hit-and-miss comic world
segments.body: Not every idea sustains itself, the review says, but the series finds inventive targets in everything from Lime-bike obsession to Dubai chocolate and a man beset by snakes. Its crowded guest cast includes Steve Coogan, Jamie Demetriou and Katy Wix, though White and Demetriou remain its brightest lights.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors loses momentum after its early shocks
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors struggles to keep its early spark
content.standfirst: A review argues that the celebrity edition has become too polite to deliver the deceit its format needs. After dramatic early departures, the remaining players’ reluctance to lie or risk their public image has left the series feeling like a slog.

image.caption: Maya Jama in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: The Celebrity Traitors has lost its spark – and I know exactly why

segments.body: The review says The Celebrity Traitors has lost the excitement that made its first series compelling. It credits Alan Carr’s winning mix of mischief and apparent innocence with setting a high bar, then argues that this year’s cast has been too conscious of its public image to create the same chaos.

segments.title: A game that needs players to play
segments.body: Richard E Grant’s early admission that he was a Traitor and the subsequent banishment of Myha’la provided a burst of drama. Since then, the review says, reluctant Traitors and overly apologetic Faithfuls have drained the show of momentum. It hopes the remaining players will embrace deception rather than simply try to remain likeable.

content.headline: Time returns to a young offenders’ institution to examine masculinity
content.shortHeadline: Time’s new series examines anger and masculinity in prison
content.standfirst: Jimmy McGovern’s third series follows boys held in a young offenders’ institution and the adults charged with supervising them. The review connects the show’s violence to isolation and a prison system with fewer routes to education and support.

image.caption: David Tennant as prison officer Bobby Bailey in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time picks up where Adolescence left off

segments.body: The new series of Time is set in a young offenders’ institution, where teenage boys live in single cells and face the whims of prison officers. The review describes an environment marked by anger and violence, with even the softer-spoken inmates caught in its power struggles.

segments.title: A system that leaves people isolated
segments.body: The officers are not outside the show’s portrait of harmful masculinity: one uses violence to assert authority, while another struggles to express emotion. A prison officer recalls that earlier provision included a library, training and education; now, he says, inmates can be locked in their cells for 23 hours a day. The review sees isolation as a condition in which resentment grows.

content.headline: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings a lively holiday mood to the living room
content.shortHeadline: Switch Sports Resort makes family play feel like a holiday
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s collection adds new sports, a resort to explore and small touches of atmosphere to the Switch Sports formula. A review finds it easy to pick up with friends and family, with enough variety to keep younger players returning.

image.caption: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.

sources.originalTitle: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games

segments.body: Switch Sports Resort brings back tennis, bowling and volleyball, then adds golf, basketball and seven new activities, including archery, skateboarding and jetskiing. The review finds most sports intuitive within a few attempts, with a deliberately silly edge—thumb wrestling, for example, gives characters oversized thumbs.

segments.title: A place to return to
segments.body: The island can be explored by jetski or small plane, with beaches, cafés and stadiums giving the collection a stronger sense of place than a simple menu of activities. Unlockable outfits and variations on the sports offer reasons to keep playing alone, while the reviewer’s family experience suggests it also works as a shared living-room game.

content.headline: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 puts character and consequence inside the action
content.shortHeadline: Modern Warfare 4 makes its campaign about people in the battle
content.standfirst: The game’s campaign links a South Korean soldier’s unit to Captain Price’s pursuit of Makarov. Its narrative director explains how the developers tried to make large battles matter through character, player choice and cultural consultation.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 combines large-scale battles with a character-led campaign.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon

segments.body: Modern Warfare 4 opens with a fictional North Korean invasion of South Korea. Players follow conscripted soldier Park Hyun Jun and his inexperienced unit as cities come under attack, while a second plot follows Captain John Price and cartel boss Valeria Garza in pursuit of Makarov. The two strands drive the campaign towards a connected finale.

segments.title: Building story into play
segments.body: Narrative director Jeff Negus says the team aimed to combine quieter character moments with large-scale action, so that a gameplay mechanic could feel necessary to the story rather than added on. He says the studio consulted military and cultural advisers, including a dialect coach familiar with differences between North and South Korean speech.

perspectives.body: Negus frames the campaign’s method as a partnership between player and protagonist: action matters more when the player understands the people caught in it, he says, and the story was revised and tested as its levels took shape.

content.headline: Ubisoft Paris moves from Mario to tactical combat with Rainbow Six Tactics
content.shortHeadline: Rainbow Six Tactics takes Ubisoft Paris from Mario to military action
content.standfirst: After making Mario + Rabbids, Ubisoft Paris is turning to a turn-based spin-off of Rainbow Six Siege. Developers explain how the studio is translating the shooter’s preparation and teamwork into a slower strategy game.

image.caption: Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics.

sources.originalTitle: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics

segments.body: Rainbow Six Tactics shifts Ubisoft Paris from the bright world of Mario + Rabbids to a tactical game built around the Rainbow Six series. In a hands-on demonstration, a squad uses drones and explosives to enter a guarded warehouse, then works through a hostage extraction. The developers say preparation and consequences are central to both the shooter and the new strategy format.

segments.title: A different kind of freedom
segments.body: Creative director Elie Benhamou says players should be able to experiment rather than follow a single solution. The game’s 15 operators can approach problems in different ways, and players can arrest some enemies instead of killing them to gain intelligence. The feature also notes that turn-based tactics remain a niche genre despite a renewed run of releases.

content.headline: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse delivers vivid combat but uneven exploration
content.shortHeadline: Belmont’s Curse is thrilling in combat and uneven between fights
content.standfirst: The new Castlevania sends Rose Belmont through a demon-filled Paris and Dracula’s castle. A review praises its frenetic battles and elaborate platforming rooms, while finding the exploration and pacing inconsistent.

image.caption: Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.

sources.originalTitle: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled

segments.body: Belmont’s Curse follows Rose Belmont as she tries to free Paris from demonic occupation. The review finds the combat its strongest feature: fights are fast and demanding, and even small enemies can land heavy blows. The game favours twitch-based action over the series’ traditional role-playing elements, a change that may frustrate some longtime fans.

segments.title: A gothic world with uneven paths
segments.body: Exploration centres on challenge rooms, platforming and tools that Rose gains as she progresses. A library and a puzzle involving a magic organ show off the game’s inventiveness, but other stretches rely on less inspired combat. The review finds the game improves after Rose enters Dracula’s castle, while concluding that it never quite matches the genre’s strongest recent examples.

content.headline: A father and son rediscover their bond through a game they first played together
content.shortHeadline: A father and son reconnect through their old co-op game
content.standfirst: Years after first playing Modern Warfare 2 together, a father and his adult son revisit its co-op missions. Their uneven starts give way to shared strategy—and an unexpectedly emotional account of gaming as family time.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his 22-year-old son return to the co-op missions of Modern Warfare 2, a game they first played together when the son was five. The father moves cautiously through each level, while his son charges ahead. After repeated failures, they adjust their styles, learn to work together and finally beat missions they had left unfinished years earlier.

segments.title: Play as a way of being together
segments.body: The essay finds joy not only in winning but in the shared routines of late-night play, food and conversation. With both players facing the prospect of living in different parts of the world, the son tells his father he will remember these weeks as some of their best times together. The writer admits he turns away to hide his tears.

content.headline: A fertile Cavendish banana could open a new route to disease resistance
content.shortHeadline: A fertile Cavendish offers a new breeding route
content.standfirst: A research collaboration says it has developed a fertile Cavendish line, potentially making cross-breeding possible. The method and chromosome count have not been disclosed, and resistant, commercially viable fruit is still a goal, not a result.

image.caption: Fernando García Bastidas at work on KeyGene’s banana-breeding programme.

sources.originalTitle: Have scientists finally found a way to save the banana from disaster?

segments.title: A possible way past sterility
segments.body: Most Cavendish bananas are sterile and are propagated from offshoots, leaving crops genetically similar and vulnerable to disease. Yelloway, a collaboration between Chiquita and KeyGene, says its fertile line could allow breeders to cross Cavendish with other bananas, seeking disease resistance and other useful traits.

segments.title: A route, not yet a resistant banana
segments.body: The details of how the line was produced, including its chromosome count, have not been made public. Researchers say cross-breeding might yield disease-resistant plants, but the offspring could look and taste different from Cavendish. New varieties would still need to meet growers’ requirements for resistance, yield and flavour.

segments.title: Other approaches—and a biodiversity question
segments.body: Researchers are also pursuing a genetically modified Cavendish and gene editing. Chiquita’s sustainability director argues that improving Cavendish could preserve dependence on a monocrop rather than increase diversity. The new fertile line may offer another option, but its practical benefits remain to be demonstrated.

content.headline: Study warns Texas data centres could reverse decades of cleaner air
content.shortHeadline: Texas data centres could reverse air-quality gains
